issues.legal_issue: A late application to substitute a deceased defendant’s legal representatives and set aside abatement requires sufficient cause both for the delay in seeking to set aside abatement and for failing to substitute the representatives within the prescribed time.
material_facts: The defendant died before the suit reached decree, and the suit abated when the plaintiff did not apply to substitute his legal representatives within the prescribed period.
The plaintiff later applied both to set aside the abatement and to substitute the representatives, and the application was substantially delayed.
The subordinate court found sufficient cause for the plaintiff’s delay in applying to set aside abatement and for failing to apply for substitution in time.
issues.conclusion: Both forms of sufficient cause had to be established. The subordinate court found them established, and its order allowing the application was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII rules 4 and 9(2) and (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with sections 3 and 5 and Articles 171 and 176 of the Limitation Act, require the applicant to establish sufficient cause for the delay in applying to set aside abatement and for not bringing the legal representatives on record within time. Section 5 permits the court to admit a covered application after the limitation period if sufficient cause is shown.

predicates.late_substitution_after_abatement: A party applies to substitute a deceased litigant’s legal representatives after the proceeding has abated and the prescribed time has elapsed.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay_in_seeking_to: The applicant establishes a sufficient reason for not applying to set aside abatement within the prescribed time.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_failure_to_substitu: The applicant establishes a sufficient reason for not applying to substitute the legal representatives within the prescribed time.
predicates.late_substitution_application_may_be_all: The court may admit the delayed application and set aside the abatement.

issues.definition: When a substitution application follows abatement and the applicant establishes sufficient cause for both delays, the application may be allowed.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reweigh a subordinate court’s factual findings on sufficient cause when that question falls within the subordinate court’s jurisdiction.
material_facts: The subordinate court had jurisdiction to decide whether sufficient cause justified the delays in applying to set aside abatement and to substitute the legal representatives.
The subordinate court found sufficient cause, but the High Court disagreed with those factual findings in revision.
The dispute in revision concerned the subordinate court’s assessment of sufficient cause, not an erroneous legal determination that conferred or denied jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not interfere with the subordinate court’s factual findings in revision; its order was set aside and the subordinate court’s order restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits revision in cases involving jurisdiction, including its illegal assumption, refusal, or irregular exercise, but does not authorize correction of an ordinary error of fact or law within jurisdiction. The Court relied on Bala Krishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar, M/s A. Batchamian Sahib and Co. v. A. N. Channiah, Joy Chand Lal Babu v. Kamalaksha Chaudhury, and Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria. It distinguished Babu Ram v. Munna Lal, Hari Bhikaji v. Naro Vishvanath, Dwarka v. Union of India, and Basantilata v. Amar Nath.

predicates.civil_revision_proceeding: A party seeks revision of a subordinate court’s order.
predicates.subordinate_court_decided_sufficient_cau: The subordinate court decides whether the facts establish sufficient cause on a matter it is authorized to determine.
predicates.revisional_challenge_turns_only_on_fact_: The revisional court disagrees with the subordinate court’s factual assessment without identifying a jurisdictional error.
predicates.revisional_court_may_not_reweigh_fact_fi: The revisional court cannot interfere merely because it would assess the facts differently.

issues.definition: When a revision challenges only factual findings on a matter within the subordinate court’s jurisdiction, the revisional court cannot reweigh those findings.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may interfere with an erroneous limitation-law determination when that error causes the subordinate court to assume or refuse jurisdiction.
material_facts: The subordinate court considered the limitation rules and the plaintiff’s explanation for the delay, then exercised its authority to determine whether sufficient cause existed.
The High Court’s disagreement concerned the subordinate court’s factual assessment of sufficient cause rather than a construction or selection of a limitation provision that determined jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: An erroneous construction or application of limitation law that determines whether the subordinate court has jurisdiction may be corrected in revision, but no such error justified interference in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Limitation Act requires dismissal of a proceeding made beyond limitation, and an erroneous construction or selection of the applicable limitation provision may lead a court to assume or refuse jurisdiction, permitting revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. By contrast, section 5 leaves the question of sufficient cause to the court’s determination where that provision applies. The Court explained the jurisdictional distinction through Joy Chand Lal Babu v. Kamalaksha Chaudhury and Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria.

predicates.civil_revision_proceeding: A party seeks revision of a subordinate court’s order.
predicates.subordinate_court_misconstrued_or_misapp: The subordinate court wrongly interprets or selects a limitation rule governing the proceeding.
predicates.that_error_determined_jurisdiction: The limitation-law error causes the subordinate court to assume jurisdiction it lacks or refuse jurisdiction it has.
predicates.revisional_interference_is_permitted: The revisional court may correct the jurisdictional error.

issues.definition: A revisional court may interfere when an erroneous limitation-law determination causes the subordinate court to assume or refuse jurisdiction.
